column4: The section traces water into pasture and then debris; this ayah introduces a man with two grape gardens, date palms, and crops between them. It gives a garden-and-crop setting for the later question of what endures.

The section describes water gathering and supporting growth; this ayah says both gardens yielded fruit and a river flowed through them. It is a specific picture of water retained among productive plants.

The section says worldly growth passes and the Hereafter is more abiding; this garden owner boasts that he does not think his garden will ever perish. His claim is the direct false boundary the section's permanence distinction corrects.

The section says the Hereafter is better and more abiding; this owner doubts the Hour and imagines an even better return if he is brought back to his Lord. It shows how confidence in present abundance can displace the section's lasting measure.

Before 18:41's warning that the garden's water may sink, this ayah says the Lord may give a better garden or make the present one a slippery plain. It supplies the neighboring threat of losing the productive landscape.
After 18:41's water may become unreachable, this ayah reports the garden's fruit surrounded and its owner wringing his hands. It gives the actual loss that the preceding water warning completes.
The section contrasts waste with what benefits and remains; this ayah likens charitable giving to a grain that multiplies into many ears. It shows useful growth producing a lasting return.

The section makes a reminder conditional on benefit; this ayah describes giving without following it with reminders of favor or injury, and promises reward. It brings speech and beneficial giving into the same moral scene.

The section asks whether a reminder benefits; this ayah says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. It gives a specific verbal good that outlasts a show of material giving.

The section's rock hollows gather rainwater for growth; this ayah pictures a garden on high ground receiving heavy rain or drizzle and yielding double. It is the fruitful counterpart to 2:264's rain-washed bare rock.

The section contrasts useful growth with what is swept away; this ayah pictures a garden with rivers destroyed by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is old and dependent. It makes the loss of accumulated yield especially concrete.
The section links 13:17's valley flow by measure to the root of 87:3; this ayah says what is sent down is only by a known measure. It places the measured water scene within God's measured provision.
The section develops floodwater and cloud water; this ayah describes the sky opening with pouring water in Noah's flood. It supplies a direct Quranic flood scene.
The section describes flood-filled hollows and water gathering; this ayah says the earth burst with springs and the waters met. It adds the earth-side source to the flood's rain.
The section follows rain into useful pasture; this ayah describes blessed water from the sky bringing gardens and grain. It names another Quranic rain-fed growth scene.
This continues 50:9's blessed rain and names tall palms with clustered fruit. It makes the yield of the water scene specific.
This closes 50:9–10's rain-and-crop scene by calling its yield provision for servants and a revival of dead land. It connects water's benefit to renewal.
The section connects cloud water with pasture; this ayah sends down water and brings out varied crops, palms, gardens, and fruit. It supplies a distinct formulation of rain producing useful growth.

The section moves from water and drying pasture to the Hereafter; this ayah says rain makes dead earth stir and grow, using that visible change as evidence for resurrection. It links the land's renewal to the afterlife claim.
The section follows cloud water into valleys and grass; this ayah describes winds driving clouds until rain emerges. It adds the cloud's movement as a direct water-source scene.
This ayah adds that before the rain described in 30:48, people had been in despair. It makes the arrival of gathered water a specific reversal from lack to provision.
This follows 30:48–49's rain and says to look at how God revives the earth after its death. It connects water's growth to the section's lasting-life contrast.
The section traces cloud water to pasture; this ayah says winds drive clouds and God uses them to revive dead land. It is another direct formulation of wind, cloud, and renewed growth.
The section describes water carried from clouds into valleys; this ayah says rain is poured down from clouds. It supplies the cloud-to-ground part of a rain-fed plant sequence.
After 78:14's pouring rain, this ayah names grain and vegetation growing from it. It gives the useful growth stage before the section's pasture becomes refuse.
This continues 78:14–15's rain and vegetation with dense gardens. It makes the productive landscape created by water explicit.
The section's dictionary entries center water gathering among rocks and hollows; this ayah pairs high mountains with sweet water given to drink. It is a close mountain-and-water provision image.

After 13:17's foam-and-water parable and 13:18's response contrast, this ayah distinguishes recognizing the revealed truth from blindness and says only people of understanding remember. It continues the section's question of whether a reminder takes hold.

After 28:60 says what is with God is better and more enduring than worldly enjoyment, this ayah asks whether the person promised good will be like one given only worldly enjoyment. It carries the section's passing-versus-lasting distinction into accountability.

The section's pasture becomes debris and its proverb names what is lost; this ayah compares unproductive spending to a freezing wind that destroys a people's crop. It gives another specific image of weather carrying away a hoped-for yield.
